title: Problem Details for HTTP APIs
summary: HTTP APIs need a way to report errors, and every API once invented its own format. This document defines a "problem detail" JSON or XML object that carries machine-readable error information in HTTP response bodies, so clients can handle errors consistently. It replaces RFC 7807.

eli5.summary: When a toy breaks, a good note says what broke and how to fix it, the same way every time. This gives web services one standard note for saying what went wrong.

subtitle: A standard JSON (and XML) shape for machine-readable error details in HTTP API responses.

tldr.problem: HTTP status codes alone cannot carry enough detail about an error, and non-human clients of HTTP APIs cannot make sense of an HTML error page, so each API tended to invent its own error format.
tldr.mechanism: A problem details object has optional members (type, status, title, detail, instance) plus problem-specific extensions, sent as application/problem+json or application/problem+xml in the response content.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9457 obsoletes RFC 7807. It adds a registry of common problem types, clarifies how to handle multiple problems, and gives guidance on type URIs that cannot be dereferenced.

today: RFC 9457 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2023 that obsoletes RFC 7807. No later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem with Plain Status Codes
sections.content:
HTTP status codes cannot always say enough about an error. A person using a browser can read an HTML error page, but a program calling an HTTP API cannot. RFC 9457 therefore defines simple JSON and XML formats called problem details.

The RFC's running example is an account without enough credit. The API can answer with 403 Forbidden so that generic HTTP software such as client libraries, caches and proxies understands the general meaning. The response content then carries the specifics, such as why the request was refused and the account balance, so the client can act, for example by moving more credit into the account.

Problem details work with any status code but fit 4xx and 5xx responses best. They are not the only way to describe a problem, and the RFC says an application may already have a more suitable format. The aim is to give applications a common error format so they do not define their own or redefine the meaning of existing status codes.
sections.eli5: A sign saying only 'No' does not help much. This lets the web say 'No, because you ran out of coins, and you have 30 left,' in a way a computer can read.

sections.title: The Problem Details Object
sections.content:
The canonical model is a JSON object served as application/problem+json. It can have these members, and a member whose value has the wrong type MUST be ignored:

  • type: a URI reference identifying the problem type. Consumers MUST use it as the primary identifier. If absent it is assumed to be about:blank. Absolute URIs are RECOMMENDED, and a type URI need not be resolvable.
  • status: the HTTP status code as a JSON number. It is only advisory, and generators MUST use the same code in the real HTTP response.
  • title: a short human-readable summary of the problem type. It SHOULD NOT change between occurrences, apart from localization.
  • detail: a human-readable explanation specific to this occurrence, focused on helping the client fix it. Consumers SHOULD NOT parse it for information.
  • instance: a URI reference identifying this specific occurrence. If it can be dereferenced, the problem details can be fetched from it.

Problem types may add extension members, such as balance and accounts in the credit example. Clients MUST ignore extensions they do not recognize, which lets problem types evolve.

If an API hits several problems of different types, the RFC says it is RECOMMENDED to report the most relevant or urgent one.
sections.eli5: The note has labelled boxes: what kind of problem, the number code, a short title, the details for this time, and an ID for this exact case. A computer can skip any box it does not understand.

sections.title: Defining New Problem Types
sections.content:
A new problem type MUST document a type URI (typically with the http or https scheme), a short title, and the HTTP status code it is used with. It MAY specify use of the Retry-After header, and its URI SHOULD resolve to HTML documentation explaining how to resolve the problem.

Additional member names SHOULD start with a letter, use only letters, digits and underscore, and be three characters or longer, so they can also be serialized in formats other than JSON.

The RFC also says what problem details are not for. They are not a debugging tool for the implementation. Truly generic conditions are usually better as plain status codes, since a 403 in response to a PUT already explains itself. And they are not meant to replace an existing domain-specific error format.

The document creates the HTTP Problem Types registry for common, widely used type URIs, using the Specification Required policy. It registers one entry, about:blank, meaning the problem has no semantics beyond the HTTP status code. When used, the title SHOULD match the standard status phrase, such as 'Not Found' for 404.
sections.eli5: If you make up a new kind of note, you must give it a name, a short title and a number code, and a page that explains how to fix it. Notes for everyday problems that a plain number already explains are not needed.

sections.title: XML and Other Formats
sections.content:
Appendix B defines an equivalent XML format, served as application/problem+xml and described by a RELAX NG schema. Extension arrays and objects are written in XML by treating an element with children as an object, except that an element containing only child elements named i is an array. All of this MUST use only the one XML namespace.

Appendix C notes that problem details can be embedded in other formats, either by wrapping the JSON or XML form, such as a script tag in HTML, or by translating the model into that format's conventions. The RFC makes no specific recommendation on how.
sections.eli5: The same note can be written in a second style, XML, if a service prefers it. It says the same things in different clothes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Information put into a problem type or a generated problem must be carefully vetted. The risks are leaking details that could be exploited to compromise the system, gain access, or harm the privacy of users. Generators are encouraged not to expose implementation details such as a stack dump.

The status member duplicates the HTTP status code, so the two can disagree, for example if a proxy or cache changed the code in transit. The RFC says their relative precedence is not clear, and that generic HTTP software such as proxies, load balancers, firewalls and virus scanners is unlikely to know about or respect the status member.
sections.eli5: An error note should say enough to help, but not hand out the keys to the building. Never paste secret inner workings into it.

data.title: 403 response with problem details
data.code:
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Content-Type: application/problem+json
Content-Language: en

{
 "type": "https://example.com/probs/out-of-credit",
 "title": "You do not have enough credit.",
 "detail": "Your current balance is 30, but that costs 50.",
 "instance": "/account/12345/msgs/abc",
 "balance": 30,
 "accounts": ["/account/12345",
              "/account/67890"]
}
